why-data-should-travel-with-proofs.text: A proof connects provider data to an independently accepted ledger root at a selected chainpoint. The terminal can replace data providers while preserving its acceptance policy. In the NFT example it checks the output and its datum before checking application evidence. Signatures, ledger proofs and application proofs establish different claims. Real-world effects also require an action and settlement policy.

components-and-chain-following.text: The diagram separates anchor and ledger infrastructure, each with its own node, from application proof construction and terminal verification. A terminal is a lightweight Web2 application with cryptographic capabilities, governed by purpose and risk. Accepted anchor publications supply chain progress without a per-application follower. Verified assets can support transaction construction or off-chain displays and integrations; irreversible effects also need an action policy.

offload-computation-while-retaining-trus.text: Anchors maintain current commitments and rollback. Ledger providers additionally retain history and query views and serve evidence. These workloads can be operated separately. Follow the trust page for deployment choices and the projects page for the existing CSMT-UTXO machinery and separate cost measurements.

data-and-trust-are-separate.text: Ledger providers and Lockness application services are both untrusted for correctness. An application builder may reconstruct state and generate proofs, but the terminal verifies every required claim against the root authenticated through the exact ledger output. Substitute roots, wrong applications, invalid proofs and missing evidence cannot become accepted facts. A builder checking its own inputs does not replace terminal verification.

proof-composition.text: The root-chain diagram starts with a ledger root covering the live UTxO set, then an output and datum carrying the application root, then optional further trees. Every link needs proof and interpretation. A UTxO proof establishes membership, not independent transaction validation. The sequence now starts by discovering retained views, selecting an accepted and available chainpoint and acquiring its session. A refusal stops the read path. The terminal verifies the NFT output, requests an application proof and verifies it against the authenticated root. Ledger proofs stay off-chain; application proofs can enter redeemers.

external-effects-and-settlement.text: An irreversible effect requires a settlement condition as well as verified facts and authorization. A signed root records observation, not future canonicality. Policy defines chain depth or settlement evidence, continued ancestry and refusal or deferral on abandonment or missing evidence. Several anchors agreeing at one point do not replace settlement. The concrete policy remains open.

service-boundary.text: The ledger provider preserves transaction CBOR and required references. Applications interpret the data. History coverage must be specified before sizing the provider. Each endpoint distinguishes authenticated claims from untrusted reconstruction inputs.

decisions.text: The design reuses generic chain-following capabilities instead of creating an indexer per application. Independent trust remains separate from data provision, and terminals may delegate proof construction without delegating verification.
